traveler: Judah Loew ben Bezalel (the Maharal of Prague)
title: The Klaus and the Two-Tailed Lion: Moravia, Prague, Poznań, and the Legend That Arrived Two Centuries Late
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Posen and the Line from Worms

stops.name: Worms, the claim the family carries east
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The Jewish Encyclopedia dates the family's move from Worms to Posen 'toward the end of the fifteenth century, probably in consequence of persecution'; no charter or communal record fixes it. The 1490 date is a placeholder for ordering and is attested by nothing.
stops.campa: The Bezalel line remembers itself as a Worms family, driven east into Poland at the close of the fifteenth century. The synagogue on the Judengasse is already four centuries old when they go. What travels east with them is a name and a memory of persecution. Later devotional biography takes the ancestral claim and hardens it into a birthplace, putting the infant Loew in Worms on the night of a blood libel, his first cry scattering the accusers in the street. Loew's own writings make no such claim and say nothing whatever about Worms.
suggested_refs: The Alte Synagoge of Worms, consecrated 1034 and rebuilt through the medieval centuries
sources: Putík and Polakovič, 'Judah Loew ben Bezalel, Called Maharal' (2009)

stops.name: Poznań, the birth without a record
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no birth record survives. Reference works range from 1512 (Andre Neher, cited in Encyclopedia.com's own bibliography) to about 1526, and the Jewish Encyclopedia says only 'about the second decade of the sixteenth century.' Encyclopedia.com contradicts itself, giving approximately 1520 in its main text. The Jewish Museum in Prague uses ca. 1525. The 1520 given here is a midpoint used to order the file, not a finding.
stops.campa: A son is born to Bezalel ben Ḥayyim in the Jewish streets north-east of the Poznań market, and nobody writes the day down. He will have brothers who are scholars too, Ḥayyim, Sinai and Samson, though later writers cannot agree which of them is the eldest. Every date afterwards offered for this morning is somebody else's arithmetic, and he himself never states his birth year in any of the thousands of pages he goes on to print. The Jewish Encyclopedia, three centuries later, will place it 'about the second decade of the sixteenth century.'
suggested_refs: The medieval Jewish quarter of Poznań along ul. Żydowska and ul. Wroniecka, north-east of the Stary Rynek
sources: Encyclopedia.com, 'Low, Yehudah ben Betsalel of Prague'
Alexandr Putík and Daniel Polakovič, 'Judah Loew ben Bezalel, Called Maharal', in Path of Life (2009)

stops.name: Lublin, the teacher who may be R. Sh.
stops.date_confidence: disputed. Older biographies place him under Shalom Shakhna at Lublin before 1553; Pavel Sládek treats the identification of the 'R. Sh.' of Loew's 1589 sermon with Shakhna as tentative and notes chronological objections that remain unresolved. The 1545 date orders the segment and is not attested by any document.
stops.campa: Older lives put the young man in Lublin, in the yeshiva of Shalom Shakhna, master of the dialectical method called pilpul. If it happened it is a strange apprenticeship, because the mature Loew will attack pilpul for decades as a game played over the text rather than with it, and will build his own academy to teach otherwise. In a Passover sermon of 1589 he speaks with reverence of a teacher he names only as R. Sh. Whether that is Shakhna, and whether the two men were ever in a room together, the record does not settle.
suggested_refs: The yeshiva of Shalom Shakhna at Lublin, seat of the pilpul method Loew later attacked
sources: Pavel Sládek, 'Admiration and Fear: New Perspectives on the Personality of the Maharal', Judaica Bohemiae 52.2 (2017)

stops.name: Mikulov, the seat of the Moravian rabbinate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1553 by the Jewish Virtual Library and the Jewish Encyclopedia, following David Gans's chronicle Tsemah David; the day and month are not recorded.
stops.campa: At about thirty he takes the seat of Landesrabbiner of Moravia at Nikolsburg, under the castle rock, with a rabbinical court and an academy under his hand and the Jewish communities of the whole margraviate answerable to him. It is not a local pulpit. The office reaches across a scatter of towns that have no other common authority, and he will hold it for twenty years. David Gans, who becomes his pupil in Prague two decades later, is the one who dates the appointment, in a chronicle written forty years after the fact.
suggested_refs: The Old Synagogue (Stará synagoga) of Mikulov and the seat of the Moravian Landesrabbinat
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Mikulov, the ordinances and the district elders
stops.date_confidence: attested as an activity of the whole Moravian period, 1553-1573; the single year is an ordering device. The compilation known as the Shay takkanot, the 311 Ordinances, gathers Moravian communal legislation imperfectly and cannot all be assigned to him.
stops.campa: He sits with the district elders and legislates: how the communities are taxed, what a wedding may cost, how much silver a woman may wear in the street. Restraint of luxury is not fussiness here. A community that displays wealth invites the tax collector and then the mob, and the ordinances are drafted by men who know it. Later generations gather Moravian legislation into a body of three hundred and eleven ordinances and put his name over all of it, which is more than the evidence supports.
suggested_refs: The Shay takkanot (311 Ordinances) of the Moravian communities, compiled after his tenure
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Mikulov, the door he closes on ordination
stops.date_confidence: the ordination text is attested but undated within the Moravian period; the 1573 date is that of his departure for Prague, whose cause is nowhere documented.
stops.campa: A text surviving from his Moravian years reads as a threat of excommunication against scholars who go outside his authority to be ordained. He wants the granting of the title in one pair of hands, and he is willing to say so with the harshest instrument the community owns. Why he leaves Moravia after twenty years is recorded nowhere at all. Sládek reads the ordination document as one sign among several that his authority made enemies. The chronicles note only that in 1573 he is in Prague.
suggested_refs: The surviving Moravian text threatening excommunication over unauthorized ordination
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

segments.name: The First Prague: the Klaus and the Books

stops.name: Prague, the Klaus opened for grown men
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1573 by David Gans and by the Jewish Virtual Library, which dates the founding of 'the yeshivah called Die Klaus' to the 1573-1584 Prague period.
stops.campa: He comes to the Jewish Town and opens what Gans calls a beit va'ad la-ḥakhamim, a meeting house for scholars, remembered afterward as the Klaus. It is not a school for boys. Grown men come to it, and he sets them to the Mishnah in order, tractate after tractate, on the argument that a generation which knows only the arguments of the Talmud has never read the law those arguments are about. What he has here is a room and the men who walk into it. He holds no communal office in Prague at all.
suggested_refs: The Klaus (Kloyz) academy of the Prague Jewish Town, founded as a beit va'ad la-ḥakhamim
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, the statutes of the burial society
stops.date_confidence: attested to his first Prague period; the month is arbitrary. The ḥevra kaddisha itself was founded in 1564, nine years before his arrival, so the founding is not his and the revision is.
stops.campa: The burial society of Prague, nine years old, washes and carries and buries the community's dead, and he rewrites its statutes. He is not yet the chief rabbi of anything in this city and he is already legislating for it. The work is of a piece with the ordinances he left in Moravia, the same insistence that a community is held together by what it does in order rather than by what it believes. Under the revised statutes membership in the society is an honour and a discipline at once.
suggested_refs: The statutes of the Prague ḥevra kaddisha, founded 1564 and revised under Loew
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, Gur Aryeh at the Hebrew press
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1578 by the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Jewish Virtual Library. The press is the Gersonides (Katz) Hebrew house, which operated inside the Jewish Town; the exact shop address is not established.
stops.campa: The Gersonides press in the Jewish Town prints his first great book, a supercommentary on Rashi's commentary on the Torah: a defence, verse by verse, of the master of Troyes against readers who found him naive. Rashi is not naive, Loew argues, he is compressed, and every apparent redundancy in him is a decision. The book opens by asking why the Torah begins with creation rather than with a commandment, and answers by way of the land, the tithes and the Temple. Of everything he writes, this is the book the next generations cite most.
stops.quote: Now, you may argue that the verse is still problematic; for how does the issue of the giving of the land connect to Torah's mitzvot? This is clear, since most of the Torah's mitzvot are performed in conjunction with the Jewish people's sovereignty or dwelling in the land.
stops.quote_source: Gur Aryeh on Genesis 1:1, Sefaria Community Translation (Hebrew base: Machon Yerushalayim, 1989-1995)
suggested_refs: Gur Aryeh al ha-Torah (Prague, 1578); the five-volume Bnei Brak edition of 1972
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'
Pavel Sládek, 'The Well of Confusion', Zutot 20 (2023)

stops.name: Prague, the rabbinate that goes to another man
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and contested. Putík and Polakovič reconstruct a contested succession after Isaac Melnik's death; the Jewish Virtual Library instead records only that Loew took a second rabbinical position in 1588, after Isaac Ḥayyot's resignation. Older and revisionist accounts differ on both the mechanism and the year. 1579 is the dossier's placement, not a settled date.
stops.campa: Prague's chief rabbinate falls vacant and the elders do not give it to him. It goes to Isaac Ḥayyot, his own brother-in-law, in a manoeuvre later accounts call a rabbinical overthrow. He is by now the most formidable mind in the city and he holds no position in it. The episode is legible for the rest of his life: learning and appointment are two separate currencies in Prague, and the elders pay in the second. The two men are married into the same family, and they will spend the next decade circling the same chair.
suggested_refs: The contested Prague chief rabbinate after the death of Isaac Melnik
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Kraków, Gevurot ha-Shem printed in Kazimierz
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1582 by the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Jewish Virtual Library. The pin is Kazimierz, where sixteenth-century Hebrew printing in Kraków was done; nothing records Loew travelling with the manuscript.
stops.campa: His theology of the Exodus is printed across the river in Kazimierz, among the Hebrew presses of Kraków. The book takes miracle as its subject, the moment when the fixed order of nature is suspended for the sake of a people, and it announces a projected architecture in six parts covering the whole of divine action. He completes some of it and never the rest. The reason he gives for retelling the Passover night every year is not a reason about God.
stops.quote: It is true that we are incapable of 'telling the mighty acts of God and proclaiming all God's praise.' The reason we speak of God's mighty acts on Passover eve is not for God's sake but for our own sake. We recite these praises so that we don't become ungrateful for the miracles and wonders that God has performed for us.
stops.quote_source: Gevurot ha-Shem, ch. 1, trans. Rabbi Mark Greenspan (via Sefaria)
suggested_refs: Gevurot ha-Shem (Kraków, 1582), first part of the projected six-part series
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, the sermon against the Nadler slander
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Sabbath of Repentance in 1583, which falls between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur; the Gregorian day is not fixed in the sources and September is an approximation.
stops.campa: On the Sabbath between the New Year and the Day of Atonement he preaches against a single word, Nadler. It is a slur running through Prague that a given family's descent is impure, and it works by insinuation, needing no evidence and answering to none, breaking off marriages in a community where descent is a household's only capital. He preaches against the whisper rather than against any particular whisperer. The sermon goes to the press the following year as Derush na'eh le-Shabbat Teshuvah.
suggested_refs: Derush na'eh le-Shabbat Teshuvah (Prague, 1584), the printed Nadler sermon
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'
Elchanan Reiner, 'Lineage and Libel: Maharal, the Bezalel Family, and the Nadler Affair'

stops.name: Prague, eleven scholars and the ban
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1584 by the Jewish Virtual Library, which records Loew joining ten other Prague scholars in the ban; the day is not given.
stops.campa: He gathers ten other scholars of the city and they pronounce the ban together: whoever circulates the slander is cut off. It is the heaviest weapon a Jewish community owns and they aim it at a rumour. His argument is that a rumour about lineage does what no imperial decree can do, which is to make Jews unmarriageable to one another. The printed sermon appears in the same year, and support for the campaign begins to arrive from rabbis outside Bohemia altogether.
suggested_refs: The communal ban of eleven Prague scholars against the Nadler slander, 1584
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, the base lost
stops.date_confidence: attested only as an interval. The Jewish Virtual Library records 1584-1588 as 'rabbi in Moravia or Posen'; whether he left Prague or lost his position, and why, is not documented anywhere. The month is arbitrary.
stops.campa: In the same year as the ban he stops being in Prague. The community that passed him over for the chief rabbinate keeps its arrangements and its silence, and the Klaus goes on without him. For four years the record thins almost to nothing, and the man who reappears in it is in Moravia again, a full decade after leaving the office he held there. Was he pushed out, did the Nadler campaign make his position impossible, or did an offer reach him from somewhere else? No source says.
suggested_refs: The four-year gap of 1584-1588 in Loew's documented biography
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

segments.name: The Moravian Interval and the Return

stops.name: Prostějov, documented again in Moravia
stops.date_confidence: attested by archival evidence cited in Putík and Polakovič (2009); that paper could not be fetched directly for this pass, academia.edu returning 403, so the date rests on the dossier's citation of it plus the corroborating 1584-1588 interval in the Jewish Virtual Library.
stops.campa: The documents put him in Prossnitz, a Moravian town with a substantial Jewish community, some sixty miles north of the seat he held at Nikolsburg thirty years earlier. He is in his sixties. The seat at Nikolsburg has had another man in it for fourteen years. He has printed three books and lost a rabbinate, and he is back in the province where he started, without the office he started with. No surviving source says what he does here, or what he lives on.
suggested_refs: The Jewish community of Prostějov (Prossnitz), Moravia, in the 1580s
sources: Putík and Polakovič (2009), cited through the research dossier
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prostějov, the letter that finds him
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter survives in the Wrocław University Library collection, dated 1588 and cited in Putík and Polakovič (2009). Read here through the dossier's list of archives, not from the manuscript itself.
stops.campa: A letter carrying greetings to him reaches Moravia and survives, four centuries later, in a library in Wrocław. It is a small thing and it does more work than the encyclopedias do, because it shows that a man with no chair and no city is still addressed from a distance as somebody whose good opinion is worth having. The genealogy his descendants print in the next century is full of invention; this scrap of paper is not. Nothing of its contents is quoted in the reachable literature, and what survives to be reported is the address.
suggested_refs: The 1588 letter of greeting to Loew in Moravia, Wrocław University Library
sources: Wrocław University Library holdings, as listed in the research dossier

stops.name: Gniezno, the coalition of the rabbis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Elchanan Reiner traces a transregional coalition supporting the anti-Nadler campaign, reaching from Prague through Poznań to Gniezno and including Mordecai Jaffe; the 1588 date and the individual adherences are Reiner's reading of the affair, not a dated act.
stops.campa: The campaign against the lineage slander does not stop at the Bohemian border. Rabbinic authorities in Poznań and in Gniezno lend their names to it, Mordecai Jaffe among them, and the ban acquires the reach of a network instead of the reach of a single community. Loew at this point is a rabbi without a pulpit, running a jurisdictional operation across three countries by letter, and holding no office in any of them. Reiner reads the coalition as evidence of his standing.
suggested_refs: Reiner's reconstruction of the transregional rabbinic coalition against the Nadler libel
sources: Elchanan Reiner, 'Lineage and Libel: Maharal, the Bezalel Family, and the Nadler Affair'

stops.name: Prague, the Klaus again and the Frenchmen at the desk
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested by a surviving friendship-book entry dated 1588; the month is arbitrary. His resumption of a Prague rabbinical position in the same year is attested by the Jewish Virtual Library, following Isaac Ḥayyot's departure or resignation.
stops.campa: Isaac Ḥayyot goes and Loew comes back, taking a rabbinical position in Prague again after four years away. In the same year two Frenchmen walk into his academy: Jacques Bongars, a Protestant diplomat and philologist, and Guillaume Le Normant de Trougny, who want to read the Hebrew Bible and are handed to a scholar of the house named Judah Seligmann. A friendship album records it. The episode sits badly against Loew's own written position, which grants gentiles the Noahide commandments and no share in Torah past them.
suggested_refs: The friendship-album (album amicorum) entry recording the Bongars and Le Normant visit of 1588
sources: Joanna Weinberg, 'The Maharal of Prague and the Republic of Letters', Tablet Magazine
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Kraków, Derekh ḥayyim printed in Kazimierz
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1589 by the Jewish Encyclopedia and the Jewish Virtual Library. Pinned to Kazimierz, seat of Isaac ben Aaron Prostitz's Hebrew press; a coordinate in the Kraków Rynek circulating for this item is wrong and has been dropped.
stops.campa: Isaac Prostitz's press in Kazimierz prints his commentary on Pirkei Avot, the tractate of maxims, and it turns into his book about education: what a teacher owes a pupil, what human nature will and will not bear, why a child is led rather than driven. Of the tractates it is the one with no law in it at all, and he treats it as a manual for the man at the front of the room, setting down what the room has taught him. He is nearly seventy. He has been running an academy for the better part of forty years.
suggested_refs: Derekh ḥayyim on Pirkei Avot (Kraków, 1589), printed by Isaac ben Aaron Prostitz
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, the Passover sermon and the initials R. Sh.
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1589 and to the Sabbath ha-Gadol, the Sabbath before Passover, which falls in late March or April; the exact Gregorian day is not given by any source consulted.
stops.campa: On the Sabbath before Passover he preaches in Prague, and the printed sermon carries a passing reference to a teacher he calls only R. Sh., spoken of with a deference he shows almost no other authority of his own century. Sládek proposes Shalom Shakhna of Lublin, dead more than thirty years by then, and in the same breath says the chronology is uncomfortable. He assumed the room knew who was meant, and the printed text never explains the initials anywhere.
suggested_refs: The printed Sabbath ha-Gadol sermon of 1589 and its reference to 'R. Sh.'

stops.name: Prague Castle, the audience with Rudolf II
stops.date_confidence: attested, day disputed. The Jewish Virtual Library gives 16 February 1592 and the Jewish Encyclopedia gives 23 February 1592, both rendering the Hebrew 3 Adar 5352. The earlier of the two is used here and the discrepancy is not resolved. The pin is the canonical Prague Castle audience coordinate used elsewhere in the atlas.
stops.campa: He climbs to the castle with his brother Sinai and his son-in-law Isaac Katz and is received in private by the Holy Roman Emperor. A courtier remembered as Prince Bertier is in the room. It is the single documented contact between the rabbi and the emperor, and nobody sets down who asked for it or what either man wanted from the other. David Gans, the only contemporary who reports the meeting at all, writes that the matters discussed were sealed, hidden and concealed, and stops there.
suggested_refs: David Gans's notice of the audience of 3 Adar 5352 in Tsemah David
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague Castle, what the storytellers put in the silence
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. Attached by later story-cycles to the attested audience of 1592 and dated here to that day for ordering only. No source contemporary with Loew describes any content of the meeting, and none of the marvels below appears in print before the nineteenth century.
stops.campa: Gans left a hole where the conversation should be, and three centuries of storytellers fill it. In their versions the rabbi calls up the patriarchs in front of Rudolf, or shows him distant scenes on a wall, or wins a decree against the blood libel by a demonstration the emperor cannot answer. An emperor who collected alchemists, astronomers and cabalists makes a good host for such a story. Not one line of it stands in any source before the eighteen hundreds.
suggested_refs: Gershom Scholem, 'The Idea of the Golem'; Moshe Idel, Golem (1990); Jewish Museum Berlin, online Golem exhibition, chapter 4
sources: Jewish Museum Berlin, online catalogue, 'Legendary Prague'
Research dossier synthesis of golem-legend scholarship

stops.name: Poznań, leaving Prague for the yeshiva
stops.date_confidence: attested by David Gans to 4 Iyyar 5352; the Gregorian equivalent of 16 April 1592 is the dossier's conversion. The title and the territorial scope of the office are disputed, and 'chief rabbi of all Poland' is flagged in the literature as an inflation of Gans's wording.
stops.campa: Two months after the audience he leaves Prague for Poznań, to head the yeshiva and the rabbinical courts of the city he was probably born in. He goes on the fourth of Iyyar, which is how Gans dates it, seventy years after somebody in these same streets failed to write down his birth. Scholars now read the move as a swap: Mordecai Jaffe takes the Prague seat and Loew takes the Polish one. Later writers promote the office to chief rabbi of all Poland, which is more than Gans's sentence will carry. At something past seventy he is still taking a better job. He goes.
suggested_refs: The exchange of positions between Loew and Mordecai Jaffe, reconstructed in Putík and Polakovič (2009)
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Poznań, the sermons on Torah and worship
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1593; delivered in Poznań and printed in Prague by his son-in-law Isaac Katz. Surviving copies vary in the title, so even the text's own self-description is not stable.
stops.campa: He preaches twice on the Torah, the commandments and the service of God, and the sermons travel back to Prague to be printed by his son-in-law. Isaac Katz has been setting his father-in-law's work for years and stood beside him in the emperor's room. Variation in a title is ordinary for the period, and it is a warning about everything else in the record: even a book he printed himself, in his own lifetime, over his own name, comes down in more than one shape. The surviving copies do not agree with each other about what this one is called.
suggested_refs: Drush 'al ha-Torah ve-'al ha-mitzvot (Prague, 1593), title variable across surviving copies
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Poznań, the ruling for a chained wife
stops.date_confidence: attested by the imprint Pesak 'al 'agunah (Prague, 1594); the case itself is undated and the woman is unnamed in the reachable literature.
stops.campa: A woman whose husband has vanished cannot remarry, and in Jewish law she remains that way, an agunah, a chained wife, until the death is established. Loew issues a ruling in such a case from the Poznań court and it is printed in Prague. The great books on exile and messianic redemption are still ahead of him; this is the other half of the work, one court and one marriage and an old man looking for the grounds to let her go. In the surviving bibliography the case is undated and the woman is not named.
suggested_refs: Pesak 'al 'agunah (Prague, 1594)

stops.name: Prague, the thirty-three paths at the press
stops.date_confidence: corrected. Netivot olam was printed in Prague across 1595-1596 per the English Wikipedia works list, not in 1596 alone as the Jewish Encyclopedia has it; that encyclopedia's 'Netibot Shalom' is a separate title and not an older transliteration of this one. Printed while he held the Poznań seat.
stops.campa: While he is in Poland his press in Prague sets Netivot olam, thirty-three essays on the paths a life is conducted along: Torah, worship, charity, truth, silence, modesty, shame, wealth. There is no narrative in it and no system announced anywhere. Each path is taken up on its own terms and followed until it runs out. The printing takes two years, and this is the book by which he is read as a moralist rather than as a theologian. Silence gets a path of its own. So does shame.
suggested_refs: Netivot olam (Prague, 1595-1596), thirty-three ethical discourses
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Judah Loew ben Bezalel', works list

stops.name: Prague, the chair he was refused
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier gave 'probably after 1597'; the English Wikipedia article on Mordecai Jaffe records the two men exchanging rabbinic positions in 1596, Jaffe moving to Posen and dying there in 1612. The 1597 Vienna document then confirms an office already held. Best given as 1596/97.
stops.campa: Jaffe goes to Poznań and Loew comes back to Prague, and this time the office is his in law and not only in reputation. The chair carries the whole judicial authority of the community, and he has been exercising most of it without the chair for twenty-three years. He is roughly seventy-five. Between the first refusal of this chair and the holding of it lie seventeen years, two provinces and nine printed books. Nothing in the record says the community changed its mind about him. What changed was who else was available.
suggested_refs: The Loew and Jaffe exchange of rabbinic positions, 1596
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, the signature on the imperial document
stops.date_confidence: attested. The document is dated 1597 and survives in the Austrian State Archives in Vienna, reproduced and discussed in Putík and Polakovič (2009). Loew signed it in Prague; he is not recorded as ever having gone to Vienna, and no stop is placed there.
stops.campa: A document drawn up in 1597 names him the highest-ranking rabbi of the Jews of Prague and carries his signature at the foot of it. It is dated within a year of his return and it settles the question of whether the office was ever formally his. Nearly everything else known about his life comes through a chronicle, or through a family genealogy composed a century later by a descendant with a case to make. This is an administrative paper with his own hand at the foot of it. It sits today in an archive in Vienna.
suggested_refs: The 1597 document naming Loew highest rabbi of Prague's Jews, Austrian State Archives, Vienna
sources: Putík and Polakovič, 'Judah Loew ben Bezalel, Called Maharal', in Path of Life (2009)

stops.name: Prague, Be'er ha-golah answers the historian
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1598 by the Jewish Encyclopedia's works list and corroborated by the Jewish Virtual Library's 1598-1600 cluster of publications. The funeral sermon for Akiva Günzburg of Frankfurt is printed in the same year.
stops.campa: Azariah de' Rossi had gone through the sages' stories with the equipment of a Renaissance historian and found them, in places, wrong about the world. Loew answers with a book. The aggadot are not bad natural science, he argues; they were never natural science at all, and a reader who takes them at their surface has mistaken the genre rather than caught the rabbis out. He argues it without much courtesy. He also mostly declines to name the man he is arguing with.
suggested_refs: Be'er ha-golah (Prague, 1598); Azariah de' Rossi, Me'or 'Einayim (Mantua, 1573)
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Venice, Tif'eret Yisra'el printed in the ghetto
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1599 by the Jewish Encyclopedia's works list. The book is printed in Venice; there is no evidence that Loew travelled to Italy, and this stop records the movement of the text, not of the man.
stops.campa: His book on the nature of Torah and the commandments comes off a press in the Venetian ghetto, the only one of his major works printed outside Central Europe. He does not go there and nothing suggests he ever crossed the Alps. Hebrew books travel where their authors do not, down the trade routes and back again, and a Prague manuscript is set in Italian type by compositors who have never seen the man. Its first chapter puts Israel outside the created order of nature.
stops.quote: The natural world was created in the seven days of creation - corresponding with the seven natural days are the seventy nations - for each day 10. There is one nation which is above nature and that corresponds to the eighth which is above nature.
stops.quote_source: Tif'eret Yisra'el, ch. 1, Sefaria Community Translation
suggested_refs: Tif'eret Yisra'el (Venice, 1599); the Hebrew presses of the Venetian ghetto

stops.name: Prague, Netzaḥ Yisra'el and the reading of exile
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1599 by the Jewish Encyclopedia's works list. The relation to the Zohar is a reconstruction: the dossier reports that Loew's writing often parallels kabbalistic patterns while rarely citing the Zohar explicitly, and no direct citation is claimed here.
stops.campa: He writes his book about exile past the age of seventy-five, and it opens with a rule of method: a thing is known through its opposite, so redemption cannot be discussed until destruction has been. Then he reads the whole condition of the Jews as a structure with a term to it, four kingdoms and an end. His symbolism runs close to the patterns of the Zohar that Moses de Leon put into circulation in Castile three centuries earlier, printed in Italy in his own lifetime, a book he seldom names.
stops.quote: When a good thing is known from its opposite, that is true knowledge. The knowledge of all things is acquired from their opposite. It is from the appearance of black that one can gain knowledge of the appearance of white... Therefore, we cannot explain the concept of the final redemption [geulah], without explaining the concept of exile [galut] and churban [destruction of the temple in Jerusalem].
stops.quote_source: Netzaḥ Yisra'el, ch. 1, Sefaria Community Translation (Hebrew base ed. Yehoshua D. Hartman, Machon Yerushalayim, 1997)
suggested_refs: Netzaḥ Yisra'el (Prague, 1599); the Cremona and Mantua printings of the Zohar, 1558-1560
sources: Research dossier section on Loew's kabbalistic symbolism

segments.name: The Last Books and the Grave

stops.name: Kolín, the son's grave under the vine
stops.date_confidence: attested by the surviving tombstone in the Old Jewish Cemetery at Kolín, which dates the death to 1599; secondary sources sometimes round it to 1600. The month is arbitrary. Coordinates corrected from the Czech Wikipedia figure for the cemetery.
stops.campa: Bezalel ben Judah Loew, rabbi of Kolín and his only known son, dies forty miles east of Prague and is buried there. The father is nearly eighty, in the middle of his most productive stretch, with three books through the press in twelve months, and he will outlive the son by ten years. The daughters have married into the good families of Prague and the line goes on through them. There is no record of the father travelling east to the burial. The stone over the son is a Renaissance one, carved with a grape vine.
suggested_refs: The Renaissance grape-vine tombstone of Bezalel ben Judah Loew, Old Jewish Cemetery, Kolín
sources: Putík and Polakovič (2009), on the Kolín tombstone
Czech Wikipedia, 'Starý židovský hřbitov v Kolíně'

stops.name: Prague, the last two imprints
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1600 by the Jewish Encyclopedia's works list; the two titles are often bound together in surviving copies.
stops.campa: Or ḥadash, on Esther and Purim and the hand that works the story without appearing in it, and Ner mitzvah, on Hanukkah and the four kingdoms, come off the press together and are usually bound as a single volume. One is about a queen in a book that never names God, the other about eight days of oil and four empires. They are the last books he sees printed. He has nine years left and goes on writing through them, on the narrative parts of the Talmud, in manuscript, with no press waiting on the result.
suggested_refs: Or ḥadash and Ner mitzvah (Prague, 1600), commonly bound as one volume
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Judah Loew (Liwa, Loeb) ben Bezalel'

stops.name: Prague, the aggadot written in a failing hand
stops.date_confidence: attested manuscripts, undated. The Ḥiddushei aggadot survive in the Oppenheim collection at the Bodleian Library, Oxford, carrying his own revisions; Sládek reads the deteriorating handwriting cautiously as failing eyesight and declines to make it a diagnosis. The 1606 date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: In his eighties he works through the narrative passages of the Talmud, the aggadot, the material he had defended in print against the historians, and writes a commentary on it that he never prints. The sheets carry his own corrections. Across them the writing gets worse. Sládek, who has read the manuscripts, will say only that this may be the eyesight going and refuses to call it more than that. The copies reach Oxford a century later in a collector's library.
suggested_refs: Ḥiddushei aggadot manuscripts, Oppenheim collection, Bodleian Library, Oxford
sources: Sládek's manuscript study, cited in the research dossier

stops.name: Prague, the ruling on ḥalitzah
stops.date_confidence: attested to circa 1608 by the imprint of Pesakim bi-devar ḥalitzah; the year is given as approximate in the bibliography and the day is unknown.
stops.campa: Rulings on the ceremony of ḥalitzah, by which a childless widow is released from the obligation to marry her dead husband's brother, are printed under his name. He is close to ninety, and has been issuing rulings of this kind since the Moravian court more than fifty years back. The last datable act of his working life is procedural, and the procedure is old and physical: the shoe, the loosened strap, the fixed words, the spitting, and the exact conditions under which a woman is free to leave.
suggested_refs: Pesakim bi-devar ḥalitzah (Prague, ca. 1608)

stops.name: Prague, the death and the count of dates
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 Elul 5369, which converts to 17 September 1609 Gregorian and 7 September Julian. The Jewish Encyclopedia's 22 August 1609 is an outlier and appears to be simply wrong. A supposed third date of 7 September 1609 came from misreading the Jewish Museum in Prague's page, which gives 7 September 2009, 18 Elul 5769, as the four-hundredth anniversary.
stops.campa: He dies in Prague on the eighteenth of Elul, no cause recorded, having held the office he was passed over for thirty years earlier for about twelve of them. Nobody sets down who was in the room. The reference books then disagree about the day for four centuries: 22 August in the Jewish Encyclopedia, 7 September and 17 September elsewhere, the last two being one day counted in two calendars. Only the Hebrew date is stable, and the Hebrew date is the one cut into the stone.
suggested_refs: The conversion of 18 Elul 5369 to 17 September 1609 Gregorian, 7 September Julian
sources: Jewish Museum in Prague, Path of Life catalogue page

stops.name: Old Jewish Cemetery, the lion with two tails
stops.date_confidence: attested; the tumba survives as site number 8 on the cemetery plan. That the monument is shared with his wife is reported in the dossier but was not confirmed in the cemetery article fetched for this pass, and is carried as reconstruction. The burial day is the day following the death by ordinary practice, not by a document.
stops.campa: He is buried in the crowded ground at Josefov under a house-shaped stone, a tumba rather than a slab, carved with grapes and with a lion whose two tails cross. The lion is his name, Loew, Leib, and it is also the lion of Bohemia on the royal arms, which has two tails and no other owner. The stone is number eight on the plan of a ground so crowded that the dead lie in layers. Tradition says his wife lies with him and follows within months. Visitors still fold paper into the cracks of the stone.
suggested_refs: The tumba of Judah Loew, site no. 8, Old Jewish Cemetery, Prague
sources: Jewish Museum in Prague, Path of Life catalogue page

stops.name: Old Jewish Cemetery, the genealogy written a century later
stops.date_confidence: attested printing date for Meir Perels's Megillat yuḥasin, Żółkiew 1745, more than 135 years after Loew's death. That it introduced systematic distortions into the family record is the finding of Putík and Polakovič (2009), cited here through the dossier. This stop is placed at Loew's grave, not at the Żółkiew press.
stops.campa: A descendant named Meir Perels writes the family's genealogy and has it printed at Żółkiew, and for the next two hundred years every life of the Maharal is built on it: the ancestry, the marriage, the wonders around the birth. Perels is writing about his own family and has a case to make. The Prague of stone and paper, the tumba and the 1597 signature, says far less than he does, and it is the part that holds. Modern archival work goes back to the documents and finds him inventing steadily.
suggested_refs: Meir Perels, Megillat yuḥasin (Żółkiew, 1745); the archival correction in Path of Life (2009)
sources: Putík and Polakovič, 'Judah Loew ben Bezalel, Called Maharal' (2009)

stops.name: Vltava riverbank, the clay man
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. No source contemporary with Loew, including his own writings, his pupils and his epitaph, connects him to a golem. Attribution appears in print from the 1830s: Berthold Auerbach in 1837, Gustav Philippson and Franz Klutschak in 1841, Abraham Tendlau in 1842, Leopold Weisel in 1847, with a couple of earlier instances known from 1834 and 1836. The 1847 date marks Weisel's version, the most influential early one and not the first.
stops.campa: Two and a quarter centuries after his death, storytellers put him on the mud of the Vltava at night, shaping a man out of river clay and starting him with a divine name, or with the word emet written on his forehead, to guard the Jewish Town against the blood libel. Golem traditions had circulated for centuries with no fixed maker and no fixed city; here they acquire both. Berthold Auerbach prints a version in 1837. Leopold Weisel prints in 1847 the one everybody afterward copies.
suggested_refs: Leopold Weisel, 'Der Golem', in Wolf Pascheles, Galerie der Sippurim (Prague, 1847)
sources: Edan Dekel and David Gantt Gurley, 'How the Golem Came to Prague', Jewish Quarterly Review 103.2 (2013)

stops.name: Old-New Synagogue attic, the body that is not there
stops.date_confidence: attested searches, legendary object. A renovation in 1883 and an exploration of the attic in August 2014 both found no trace of a golem. The lowest three metres of the external stairway have been removed and the attic is closed to the public. Coordinates corrected to the English Wikipedia figure for the synagogue.
stops.campa: The story says the thing was shut down and its remains carried up to the attic of the Old-New Synagogue and covered with worn-out sacred books. The lowest three metres of the outside stairway have been taken away, so nobody goes up casually. Workmen renovating in 1883 looked. An exploration in August 2014 looked again. There is no body. A further legend has a German officer climbing up during the occupation and dying of it; the record has the Gestapo never entering the attic.
suggested_refs: The sealed attic of the Old-New Synagogue and the searches of 1883 and August 2014
sources: Jewish Museum Berlin, online Golem exhibition, 'Legendary Prague'

stops.name: Prague, the wonders ascribed to the Maharal
stops.date_confidence: attested publication year, contested imprint. Nifla'ot Maharal is usually cited as Piotrków 1909, but the English Wikipedia article on Yudel Rosenberg gives Podgórze, Kraków; the imprint is not secure and no stop is pinned at either press. The Metz manuscript provenance is a hoax by scholarly consensus.
stops.campa: Yudl Rosenberg prints a cycle of golem stories and presents it as an old manuscript by Loew's son-in-law Isaac Katz, recovered from a royal library in Metz. There is no such manuscript and no such holding. The villain cardinal never existed. The audience with the emperor is dated to 1573, when the emperor was Maximilian and not Rudolf. Rosenberg had also lifted an episode from Arthur Conan Doyle by way of a Russian translation. Within six years Paul Wegener is filming it.
suggested_refs: Yudl Rosenberg, Nifla'ot Maharal mi-Prag 'im ha-Golem (1909), trans. Curt Leviant, Yale University Press, 2007; Paul Wegener's Golem films, 1915, 1917, 1920
sources: Shnayer Leiman, 'The Adventure of the Maharal of Prague in London'
Internet Archive record, The Golem and the Wondrous Deeds of the Maharal of Prague (2007)

stops.name: Prague, the statue at the corner of the new city hall
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1917. The statue is by Ladislav Šaloun and stands on the Nová radnice at Mariánské náměstí in the Old Town, the building completed in 1911 with the architect Osvald Polívka. It is not on the Novoměstská radnice on Charles Square, a different building a kilometre south with which the location is frequently confused.
stops.campa: Ladislav Šaloun sets a bronze Loew at the corner of the city's new municipal building, three streets from the cemetery. Osvald Polívka's building had been finished six years earlier, and the rabbi is fitted to its corner the way a saint is fitted to a cathedral. By 1917 the Czech public knows him as the maker of the golem and a magician at the emperor's court, and has read almost nothing he wrote. In the bronze he is an old man in a heavy robe, with a naked girl reaching up to him, a figure the guides explain as death arriving in disguise.
suggested_refs: Ladislav Šaloun's Rabbi Loew, Nová radnice, Mariánské náměstí 2, Prague 1

stops.name: Prague Castle, the four hundredth year
stops.date_confidence: attested. The exhibition Path of Life: Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel, ca. 1525-1609 was held at Prague Castle in 2009 with a 315-page catalogue published by Academia and the Jewish Museum in Prague; the museum's own page credits Alexandr Putík and does not name Olga Sixtová as co-editor. The anniversary of the death fell on 7 September 2009, 18 Elul 5769. A Czech Post stamp was issued in May 2009 and a Czech Mint silver coin in June; a joint Czech and Israeli stamp reproducing his tombstone had appeared separately in April 1997 and is not part of the anniversary programme.
stops.campa: Four hundred years after the burial, the castle he once climbed for an audience of unknown content houses an exhibition about him, and the catalogue that comes with it is the first serious attempt to get behind Perels: archives, municipal records, tombstones, the 1597 signature. A stamp is issued and a silver coin struck. In Israel there is a village founded by Czech survivors in 1949 and called Kerem Maharal, the Maharal's vineyard, after the grapes carved on his stone.
suggested_refs: Alexandr Putík, ed., Path of Life: Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel, ca. 1525-1609 (Academia and the Jewish Museum in Prague, 2009)
sources: Jewish Museum in Prague, exhibition catalogue page
